tei:titleStmt.tei:title: Birkas Kohanim: May our prayer be sweet before You

tei:availability.tei:p: Published by Sefaria under CC-BY, which Sefaria defines as Creative Commons Attribution 3.0.

tei:div.tei:p:
May our prayer be sweet before You as a burnt-offering and as a sacrifice. Please, Merciful One, in Your abundant mercy return Your Divine Presence to Zion, Your city, and the order of the [Temple] Service to Jerusalem. And may our eyes behold Your merciful return to Zion. And there we will serve You reverently as in the days of old, and in earlier years.
The Chazzan concludes: Blessed are You, Adonoy, You alone, in reverence do we serve.
The congregation recites Modim d'Rabbanan, on page 000. The following prayer is said silently by the Kohanim. May it be Your will Adonoy, our God and the God of our fathers, that this blessing which You have commanded us to bless Your people Israel, be a perfect blessing; that there be in it neither stumbling nor iniquity from now, forever.
The Chazzan then says: Kohanim
The Congregation responds: Your holy people, as it is said.

tei:note.tei:p: The burnt-offering refers to the עוֹלַת הַתָּמִיד , the daily communal burnt-offering, while sacrifice refers to the מוּסַף , the additional offerings of the Festivals.— Iyun Tefiloh According to Dover Shalom these two types of offerings can be compared to two kinds of prayers. The truly pious Jew is concerned only with serving his Creator and his prayers are offered entirely to God. He asks nothing for himself. His prayers are similar to a burnt-offering which is consumed in its entirety on God’s altar. Not every Jew is capable of such a lofty degree of Divine service. Many serve God but are conscious of their own personal needs and desires. Their prayer is thus similar to a שְׁלָמִים , peace offering, of which only part is consumed on the altar, the owner also being permitted to eat and enjoy part of it. We pray that both kinds of prayers be pleasing and acceptable to God, as were the sacrifices on the altar.
